$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{w}_{1}+9{w}_{2}=3 \\ -1{w}_{1}+3{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 

in the case where $A$ has a single, defective eigenvalue $\lambda$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the first fundamental solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_1(t) = \mathbf{v}  e^{\lambda t},
$$

as usual, and the second fundamental solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and $\mathbf w$ is a vector that satisfies $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

We can see that the second fundamental solution works by substituting $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}^{′}(t) & =A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}] & =A(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}) \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =Avt{e}^{\lambda t}+Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v+\lambda w & =Aw \\ v & =Aw-\lambda w \\ v & =(A-\lambda I)w.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So we conclude that $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}$ works as a second fundamental solution provided that $\mathbf w$ is a solution to $\mathbf{v}  =  (A - \lambda I) \mathbf{w}.$

**Note:**
By linearity, any linear combination of $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ is also a solution of the system. Moreover, it turns out, every solution can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t).$ Later in the course, we’ll see why certain particular solutions can generate the entire solution set." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157476 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}3-1 & 4 \\ -1 & -1-1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

"When solving the $2\times 2$ matrix differential equation 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 

in the case where $A$ has a single, defective eigenvalue $\lambda$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the first fundamental solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_1(t) = \mathbf{v}  e^{\lambda t},
$$

as usual, and the second fundamental solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}
$$

The reason why we must use this form is that if we were to guess [math]\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}[/math] as a second fundamental solution [math]\textrm x_2(t),[/math] then we would get
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x}_2'(t) &= A \mathbf{x}_2(t) \\[3pt]
\dfrac{ \textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left[ \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t} \right] &= A \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t} \\[3pt]
\mathbf{v}  e^{\lambda t}+ \lambda \mathbf{v}  t e^{\lambda t} &= \lambda \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t} \\[3pt]
\mathbf{v}  e^{\lambda t} &= 0 \\[3pt]
\mathbf{v} &= 0.
\end{align*} 

But we can't have [math]\mathbf v = \mathbf 0,[/math] since [math]\mathbf v[/math] is an eigenvector, and an eigenvector can't be the zero vector! So this guess will not work.

We can see that the second fundamental solution works by substituting $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}^{'}(t) & =A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}] & =A(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}) \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =Avt{e}^{\lambda t}+Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =\lambda vt{e}^{\lambda t}+Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v{e}^{\lambda t}+\lambda w{e}^{\lambda t} & =Aw{e}^{\lambda t} \\ v+\lambda w & =Aw \\ v & =Aw-\lambda w \\ v & =(A-\lambda I)w.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So we conclude that $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}$ works as a second fundamental solution provided that $\mathbf w$ is a solution to $\mathbf{v}  =  (A - \lambda I) \mathbf{w}.$

**Note:**
By linearity, any linear combination of $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ is also a solution of the system.
